questions.q: Once an alert is confirmed real, what does incident-scale triage add to what Lesson 3's single-alert triage already covered?
options: Nothing - confirming one alert as real always means the incident is fully understood
Replacing entity information with a single alert ID
Pulling every related alert and event tied to the incident, not just closing the one confirmed alert
A requirement to ignore any event that isn't itself an alert
questions.explain: A confirmed incident is usually a cluster of related activity, not just the first alert that fired.

questions.q: In the impossible-travel example, what did pulling events tied to the same account reveal that closing the single alert would have missed?
options: A second, unrelated user account
That the account had never signed in before
That the sign-in alert was a false positive
A mailbox forwarding rule, an OAuth app grant, and a file download, all within the same short window
questions.explain: The related events, tied to the same account, showed a confirmed account takeover with four connected actions.

questions.q: What does "grouping by entity, not by alert ID" mean in incident-scale triage?
options: Only investigating alerts that share the exact same alert ID
Assigning every alert a random new ID number
Deleting alerts that don't match a known entity
Collecting every alert and event sharing the same account, host, or IP into one working set
questions.explain: Entity-based grouping pulls together everything tied to the same user, host, or IP, which is how a real incident's full scope gets built.

questions.q: Why is closing a confirmed alert as "escalated" without pulling its related events considered a real IR failure mode?
options: Because escalated alerts are automatically deleted after 24 hours
Because single-alert triage is never actually necessary
Because the attacker may have already set up persistence, like a mail-forwarding rule, that the analyst never investigated
Because it violates a strict rule that every alert must stay open for a full week
questions.explain: Treating each alert in a cluster as its own ticket can miss a foothold the attacker already established, like a mailbox rule that survives a password reset.

questions.q: Why does incident-scale triage need to happen before containment decisions are made?
options: Because containment decisions made on an incomplete picture of what happened are decisions made on bad information
Because containment can only be performed by a different team than triage
Because containment tools require a minimum number of twelve related alerts
Because it has no real effect on containment decisions either way
questions.explain: Understanding the full cluster of related activity is what lets containment target the real scope of the incident, not just the first alert.
